messages.content: Write the engineering culture section of a careers page. Around 250 words.

## How we work

We ship small and often. Most changes reach production the same day they're written, behind a flag, and the person who wrote the change is the person watching the dashboard afterward. There's no separate operations team to hand the pager to. That arrangement sounds unfair right up until you notice what it does to your design instincts — you build things differently when you know who gets woken up.

Code review here is not a rubber stamp. Expect hard questions on your first pull request, and expect to be asking them on someone else's by your second week. We'd rather spend an afternoon arguing about an interface than spend three years living inside a bad one. But once a call is made, it's made. We write down the reasoning, link it in the repo, and stop relitigating.

Nobody counts your tickets. What we care about is whether the thing you built still works in six months and whether the next engineer can understand it without finding you on Slack.

Two standing meetings a week, both under thirty minutes. The rest of your calendar is yours. Roughly a fifth of each quarter goes to work engineers pick themselves — tooling, migrations, the refactor everyone complains about. A third of what's in production today started there.

We hire people who read the code before they rewrite it, who write plainly, and who will tell a senior engineer they're wrong. Seniority buys you more context, not more authority. Titles are for org charts.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

output:
## How we work

Changes go out in small pieces, usually the same day someone writes them, behind a flag. Whoever wrote it watches the graphs afterward. There's no ops team standing by to take the pager off your hands. It sounds like a raw deal until the first time you're the one awake at 3am. After that you start designing for whoever's on call, because it's you.

Reviews are real here. Your first pull request will get hard questions, and by week two you'll be asking them on someone else's. An afternoon of arguing about an interface beats three years stuck inside the wrong one. Once a call is made, though, it's made. The reasoning goes in writing, gets linked from the repo, and the argument is over.

Nobody counts your tickets. The questions that matter: does the thing still work in six months, and can the next person read it without pinging you on Slack.

Two recurring meetings a week, neither over half an hour. Everything else on your calendar is yours to fill. About a fifth of every quarter goes to whatever engineers decide is worth doing: tooling, migrations, the refactor everyone gripes about in standup. A third of what's running in production today started there.

We hire people who read the code before rewriting it, who write in plain sentences, and who'll tell a staff engineer to their face that they're wrong. Being senior here means you have more context, not more say. Titles exist for the org chart.
